params.title: Modulation
params.subtitle: How a voice rides on a radio wave: FM deviation, double and single sideband, the two-tone test, and pulse modulation.

onScreen: How a voice rides on a radio wave
scenes.narration: Welcome to modulation: how a transmitter puts a voice onto a radio wave. Every transmitter you'll work on does this in some way, so understanding it helps you set one up, test it and track down faults. We'll build from the basics, so you don't need any background. By the end, you'll be able to work out the deviation ratio of a frequency modulation signal and tell it apart from the modulation index. You'll know how frequency modulation, double sideband and single sideband signals are made, how to read the single sideband transmitter in Figure 3H17 and test that it amplifies a voice without distorting it, and what each kind of pulse modulation changes.

params.title: Waves, cycles and frequency
labels: 1 cycle: one full swing up, down and back
Frequency: cycles per second, in hertz (Hz). 1 kHz = 1000 Hz
Audio from a microphone: about 100 Hz to a few kHz. Radio: far higher
Carrier: a steady radio-frequency wave from an oscillator

onScreen: Frequency: cycles per second, in hertz; 1 kHz = 1000 Hz
Audio: about 100 Hz to a few kHz; radio far higher
Carrier: a steady radio wave from an oscillator
scenes.narration: First, a quick refresher on waves. A radio signal is an electrical wave: a voltage, or electrical push, that swings up, down and back again, over and over, in a smooth shape called a sine wave. One complete swing is a cycle. The number of cycles each second is the frequency, measured in hertz: 1 hertz is 1 cycle per second, and 1 kilohertz is 1000 hertz. A microphone turns your voice into an electrical wave too, called audio: a mix of frequencies from about 100 hertz up to a few thousand. Radio frequencies are far higher, often millions of cycles a second. A transmitter makes its radio wave with an oscillator, a circuit that swings steadily at one frequency, like a pendulum. That steady wave is the carrier.

params.title: Modulation: putting the audio on the carrier
items: Audio alone: would need an antenna many miles long
Each station: its own carrier frequency
Modulation: changing the carrier in step with the audio
AM, amplitude modulation: the audio changes the carrier's height
FM, frequency modulation: the audio changes the carrier's frequency

onScreen: Audio alone needs an antenna miles long
Modulation: changing the carrier with the audio
scenes.narration: Why does a transmitter need a carrier at all? Why not just send the audio itself? Audio makes a very poor radio wave: you'd need an antenna many miles long. And every station would crowd onto the same few frequencies, so you'd hear them all at once. So each station gets its own carrier frequency, and the audio rides on it. But a steady carrier holds no message. To send a voice, the transmitter changes the carrier in step with the audio. That's modulation, and the audio doing the changing is called the modulating signal. There are 2 main ways. Amplitude modulation, or AM, changes the carrier's height, its amplitude, while the frequency stays put. Frequency modulation, or FM, keeps the height steady and nudges the frequency up and down.

params.title: Making FM: audio into the oscillator

blocks.label: Amplifier supply voltage
blocks.note: Varying it gives AM, not FM

onScreen: Audio fed directly to the oscillator
Oscillator frequency swings with the audio
Varying amplifier supply voltage gives AM, not FM
scenes.narration: AM comes back later; first, how is FM made? Start with the audio from the microphone. It goes to a varactor, a tuning part whose effect changes with the voltage across it. The varactor sits in the oscillator's tuning, which sets its frequency the way a guitar string's length sets its note. So as the audio voltage rises and falls, the oscillator's frequency swings up and down in step. A reactance modulator does the same job with a different circuit. That's how an FM-phone signal, phone meaning voice, is produced: by feeding the audio directly to the oscillator. The trap is an amplifier's supply voltage. An amplifier makes a signal stronger, so varying the supply it runs on changes the output's strength, not its frequency. That gives AM instead. A balanced modulator, met later, doesn't make FM either.

params.title: FM up close: deviation
labels: Crowded cycles: higher frequency. Spread out: lower
Deviation: how far the frequency swings from center
Louder audio: bigger deviation
Modulating frequency: how often the swing repeats

onScreen: Deviation: how far the frequency swings
Modulating frequency: how often it swings
scenes.narration: Now look at the FM signal itself more closely. Where the cycles crowd together, the frequency is higher; where they spread out, it's lower. The carrier's resting frequency is its center frequency. How far the frequency moves away from the center is called the deviation, measured in kilohertz. It's written plus or minus, because the swing goes both above and below: plus or minus 5 kilohertz means up to 5 kilohertz either side. The audio controls 2 things. Its loudness sets the deviation: louder audio puts a bigger voltage on the varactor, so the frequency swings further. Its frequency, called the modulating frequency, sets how often the swing happens: a steady 1 kilohertz tone swings the carrier up and down 1000 times a second.

params.title: Modulation index: a moment-by-moment ratio
steps: Both in kHz, so the units cancel
params.answer: The index changes from moment to moment

scenes.narration: Deviation and modulating frequency combine into one number, the modulation index. It's the ratio between the deviation of a frequency modulated signal and the modulating frequency at a given time: one divided by the other. That compares how far the carrier swings with how often it swings. Both are in kilohertz, so the units cancel. Take a quiet 1 kilohertz tone that swings the carrier plus or minus 1 kilohertz: 1 divided by 1 gives an index of 1. Make it louder, swinging plus or minus 3 kilohertz, and the index jumps to 3. Raise the pitch to 3 kilohertz at that loudness, and 3 divided by 3 brings it back to 1. Speech keeps changing in loudness and pitch, so the index changes from moment to moment.

params.title: Deviation ratio: the fixed design figure
items: Deviation ratio = maximum deviation ÷ highest audio modulating frequency
Both are limits set when the FM system is designed
So it's one fixed figure for the system
Deviation on top, audio frequency on the bottom

onScreen: Deviation ratio = maximum deviation ÷ highest audio frequency
scenes.narration: A number that keeps changing can't describe a whole FM system, though. For that, there's the deviation ratio: the maximum carrier frequency deviation divided by the highest audio modulating frequency. Those are the extremes, the biggest deviation the system allows and the highest audio frequency it accepts. Both are limits built into the design, so the deviation ratio is one fixed figure for a given FM system. It doesn't wander with the speech, and those same 2 limits set how wide a slice of the radio band the signal needs. One rule to remember: deviation goes on top, audio frequency on the bottom. The exam's wrong choices turn it upside down, or bring in the carrier's center frequency or an average audio frequency instead.

params.title: Worked example 1: deviation ratio
params.formula: Deviation ratio = max deviation ÷ max audio
steps: Maximum deviation: ±5 kHz, so use 5 kHz

onScreen: Deviation ratio = maximum deviation ÷ maximum audio
scenes.narration: Now the first exam example. An FM-phone signal has a maximum frequency deviation of plus or minus 5 kilohertz, and accepts a maximum modulation rate of 3 kilohertz. For the deviation, use the size of the swing, 5 kilohertz; the plus or minus only says it goes both ways. Modulation rate is another name for the audio frequency: it's how many times a second the carrier gets swung. Now divide, deviation on top: 5 kilohertz divided by 3 kilohertz is 1.666 and so on, and the kilohertz cancel out. Divide upside down, 3 by 5, and you get the trap answer, 0.6. The right answer, as the exam lists it, is 1.66. Does that make sense? The deviation is bigger than the audio frequency, so the ratio should be more than 1, and it is.

params.title: Worked example 2: deviation ratio
params.formula: Deviation ratio = max deviation ÷ max audio
steps: Maximum swing: ±7.5 kHz, so use 7.5 kHz

scenes.narration: The second example uses the same method. This time the maximum frequency swing is plus or minus 7.5 kilohertz, and the maximum modulation rate is 3.5 kilohertz. Swing is just another word for deviation. Put the deviation on top: 7.5 kilohertz divided by 3.5 kilohertz is about 2.14. Flip it, 3.5 divided by 7.5, and you get the trap, 0.47. The other wrong choices, 0.214 and 47, are just 2.14 and 0.47 with the decimal point moved. So the answer is about 2.14, and it makes sense: above 1, because the deviation is the bigger number.

onScreen: Modulation index: deviation over modulating frequency at a given time, varies
Deviation ratio: maximum deviation over highest audio frequency, fixed
Deviation index and modulation ratio: wrong choices
scenes.narration: Now put the 2 terms side by side, because the exam likes to swap them. Both divide a deviation by an audio frequency. The modulation index uses whatever is happening at a given time, so it changes as the audio changes. The deviation ratio uses the limits, the maximum deviation and the maximum audio modulating frequency, so it's fixed for the system. If a question asks for the term for maximum deviation divided by maximum audio modulating frequency, the answer is deviation ratio, not modulation index. The word maximum is your clue, and deviation index and modulation ratio aren't the names used. If it asks what modulation index means, pick the ratio between the deviation and the modulating frequency, the choice without the word maximum.

params.title: AM up close: the envelope
labels: Fast wiggles: the carrier
The peaks rise and fall with the audio
Envelope: the outline traced by the peaks

onScreen: Envelope: the outline of the peaks
scenes.narration: That's frequency modulation done. Our next topic is single sideband, a slimmed-down form of AM, so let's look at AM properly first. Here's an AM signal. The fast wiggles are the carrier. Their height rises and falls with the audio, so the peaks trace out the shape of the audio wave. That outline, top and bottom, is called the envelope. The envelope is the message: an AM receiver simply follows it to recover the sound. Keep the word envelope in mind, because we'll use it later to test transmitters.

params.title: AM by frequency: a carrier and 2 sidebands
labels: Spectrum: the signal spread out by frequency
Center: the carrier
Upper sideband: carrier + audio. Lower: carrier − audio
Both sidebands: double sideband (DSB)

scenes.narration: There's a second way to look at the same signal. Instead of spreading it out over time, spread it out by frequency, the way a prism spreads light into colors. This view is called a spectrum. The carrier is the tall line in the middle. And it shows something surprising: modulation creates new frequencies. Modulate the carrier with a 1 kilohertz tone, and new frequencies appear exactly 1 kilohertz above and below it. A voice, a mix of many tones, makes whole bands of them. Just above the carrier is the upper sideband, a band of frequencies at the carrier plus the audio. Just below it is the lower sideband, at the carrier minus the audio. Each sideband carries a complete copy of the audio. Ordinary AM has both, so it's called double sideband, or DSB.

blocks.label: Supply voltage
blocks.note: Pushed up and down by the audio

onScreen: Reactance modulators and varactors make FM
scenes.narration: So how is a double sideband phone signal produced? By modulating the supply voltage to a class C amplifier. An oscillator makes a steady carrier, and a class C amplifier boosts it for sending. Like any amplifier, it takes its power from its supply voltage. Class C means it works in short bursts, switching on for just part of each cycle. That makes it very efficient, and its output strength follows its supply voltage closely. Now let the audio push the supply voltage up and down, and the carrier coming out grows and shrinks with it. That's ordinary AM, the AM we met as the FM trap: a carrier with 2 sidebands, a double sideband signal. A reactance modulator, or a varactor in an oscillator, makes FM instead. A phase detector, oscillator and filter in a feedback loop just holds an oscillator steady on one frequency.

params.title: Single sideband: keep only what's needed
labels: The carrier is the same whether you speak or not
The 2 sidebands are copies of the same audio
SSB: 1 sideband, carrier suppressed
All the power carries the voice, in half the bandwidth

scenes.narration: Double sideband works, but it's wasteful. The carrier is the same whether you're talking or not, so it carries no message, yet it takes a big share of the transmitter's power. And the 2 sidebands are mirror copies of the same audio. So why send all 3? Single sideband, or SSB, sends just one sideband and suppresses the carrier, meaning it's removed or reduced to almost nothing. Now all the transmitter's power goes into the part that carries your voice, and the signal takes up half the bandwidth, the width of the slice of frequencies it occupies. The receiver puts a carrier back in to recover the sound.

callouts.label: Block 1: 455 kHz crystal oscillator, supplies the carrier
Block 2: microphone, where audio intelligence is inserted
An audio amplifier carries the voice up to block 3
Block 3: balanced modulator, where audio meets carrier

scenes.narration: How does a real SSB transmitter do it? Figure 3H17 shows one, with 4 numbered blocks. Block 1 is a 455 kilohertz crystal oscillator. A quartz crystal holds an oscillator on one exact frequency, and this one supplies the carrier. SSB won't send the carrier, but it needs it to make the sidebands. Block 2, at the bottom, is the microphone. That's where the audio intelligence, meaning the information being sent, is inserted. Its audio passes through an amplifier up into block 3, the balanced modulator, where the audio meets the carrier. Further along, block 4 is the mixer. For the exam, remember 2 numbers: audio goes in at block 2, and block 4 is the mixer. Don't pick block 3: the audio reaches it, but it's inserted at block 2.

onScreen: Block 1: crystal oscillator, the 455 kHz carrier
Block 3: balanced modulator, 2 sidebands, carrier cancelled
scenes.narration: Now follow the signal through. Block 1, the crystal oscillator, sends its steady 455 kilohertz carrier along the top of the figure. Block 2, the microphone, sends the voice up from below, through its amplifier. They meet at block 3, the balanced modulator, which combines them to make the 2 sidebands. It's called balanced because its 2 halves are arranged so the carrier cancels itself out, leaving just the sidebands. That's how SSB uses the carrier without sending it. The 2 sidebands then go on to the I.F. amplifier, where one of them is removed.

params.title: Figure 3H17: up to the operating frequency

blocks.label: Block 4: mixer
blocks.note: Heterodynes up to the operating frequency

onScreen: I.F. amplifier: a filter leaves 1 sideband at 455 kHz
Block 4: mixer up to the operating frequency
scenes.narration: So what's an I.F. amplifier? I.F. stands for intermediate frequency: a fixed in-between frequency, here 455 kilohertz. A filter, a circuit that passes some frequencies and blocks others, is far easier to make sharp at one fixed frequency, so in a real transmitter a filter here removes one sideband. Next is block 4, the mixer. A mixer heterodynes: it combines the signal with another frequency to make new ones, their sum and their difference. The one kept is the operating frequency, the frequency the station transmits on. Linear amplifiers boost it and feed the antenna. So block 4 is the clue: a mixer taking a sideband signal up to the operating frequency means this schematic, or circuit drawing, is most likely an SSB radio transmitter, not an audio amplifier, a shipboard radar or a wireless network computer.

params.title: Linear amplifiers: a faithful copy
items: Linear: the output is an exact, bigger copy of the input
Double the input, double the output
An SSB signal's strength rises and falls with the voice
A non-linear stage squashes or mangles it: distortion
Class C, working in bursts, is ruled out

scenes.narration: Those last amplifiers must be linear. What does that mean? A linear amplifier makes an exact, bigger copy of its input: double the input, and the output doubles too, right up to the loudest peaks. Think of a good photocopier enlarging a drawing without warping it. Why does SSB need this? With the carrier gone, the SSB signal's strength rises and falls with your voice, and that changing strength is the message. If an amplifier squashes the loudest peaks, or mangles the quiet parts, the voice comes out distorted, changed in shape. That rules out a class C amplifier: working in bursts, its output doesn't follow its input's strength. So technicians need a way to check an SSB transmitter's amplitude linearity: whether its output strength faithfully follows its input.

params.title: The two-tone test
labels: Input: a two-tone audio-frequency sine wave
Output viewed on an oscilloscope
1 tone: a flat, constant envelope, nothing to judge
2 tones: the envelope swells and shrinks in loops

scenes.narration: That check is the two-tone test. Feed the transmitter a two-tone audio-frequency sine wave, meaning 2 pure tones at once, and view the output on an oscilloscope, an instrument that draws a signal's shape on a screen. Why 2 tones? A single tone makes an SSB transmitter put out one steady radio frequency, with a flat envelope that shows nothing about linearity. That's why a single sine wave fails, and so does whistling, which is close to one pure tone. With 2 tones, the output holds 2 radio frequencies that drift in and out of step, like 2 guitar strings slightly out of tune. Where they line up, they add to a peak; where they oppose, they cancel to zero. So the envelope swells and shrinks in loops, testing the amplifiers at every strength from zero to full.

params.title: Reading the two-tone pattern
rows: Distortion where the envelope crosses zero
Phase shift, FM percentage, sideband suppression

onScreen: Distortion at the zero crossings: non-linear
Wrong choices: phase shift, FM percentage, sideband suppression
scenes.narration: So what does a two-tone test illustrate on an oscilloscope? The linearity of an SSB transmitter. Here's how to read it. Clean, evenly shaped loops, all alike and smoothly rounded, mean the transmitter is linear. Flattened tops on the loops mean an amplifier is running out of room at the peaks. Distortion where the envelope crosses zero, between the loops, means the quiet parts are being mangled. Either fault means the transmitter is non-linear. The exam's wrong choices are carrier phase shift, percentage of frequency modulation and sideband suppression. But SSB has no carrier to shift and isn't frequency modulation, and how well the unwanted sideband is removed is a separate check. The two-tone test is about linearity.

marks.label: About 1,900 Hz
marks.note: Tone 2: not a harmonic of tone 1

scenes.narration: One question remains: which 2 tones? Non-harmonically related audio signals within the modulation passband of the transmitter, such as about 700 hertz and 1,900 hertz. The passband is the range of audio frequencies the transmitter lets through; a tone outside it wouldn't be sent. A harmonic is a whole-number multiple of a frequency: 2 times 700 hertz is a harmonic of 700 hertz. Distortion creates extra frequencies at such multiples, so if one tone were a harmonic of the other, those extras could land right on it and hide. 1,900 hertz isn't a whole-number multiple of 700, so it's safe. That rules out harmonically related tones, square waves, which jump abruptly between high and low and are full of harmonics, and 2 signals of the same frequency, which are really one tone.

params.title: Pulses: sending in bursts
labels: Pulse: a short burst, on then off
Pulses repeat at a steady repetition rate
Each pulse carries a sample of the voice
A pulse's height, width or timing can change

scenes.narration: Our last topic, pulse modulation, works quite differently, and it's behind radar and digital telephone links. Everything so far used a carrier that flows nonstop. Pulse modulation sends the message as a train of short bursts called pulses: on for a moment, then off, repeating at a steady rate called the repetition rate. How can bursts carry a voice? By sampling: measuring the voice wave at regular instants, many times a second, and letting each pulse carry one measurement. Done fast enough, the receiver can rebuild the voice from the samples, the way a film makes smooth motion from still frames. A pulse has 3 things you can change: its height, or amplitude; its length, called width or duration; and its timing, called position.

params.title: Pulse-width modulation (PWM)
items: Start with a standard pulse of a set length
The voice varies its duration at each instant
Low point in the voice wave: short pulse. High point: long
Pulse amplitude and repetition rate stay fixed
Also called pulse-duration modulation

onScreen: Low point short, high point long
scenes.narration: First, pulse-width modulation, or PWM. Every pulse starts as a standard pulse of a set length, and the voice stretches or shrinks it. Voice is sent by varying a standard pulse in duration by an amount depending on the voice waveform, the shape of the voice wave, at that instant. A low point in the wave gives a short pulse, a high point a long one. In a pulse-width modulation system, then, the modulating signal varies the pulse duration, while pulse amplitude and repetition rate stay fixed. Since duration means how long a pulse lasts, this is also called pulse-duration modulation. Modulation that varies the duration of the transmitted pulse is pulse-width modulation, not pulse-height, which would mean changing the amplitude.

params.title: Pulse-position modulation (PPM)
items: Every pulse has the same width and amplitude
Each pulse has a normal moment to occur
The voice shifts it earlier or later
So the signal varies the time each pulse occurs
Pulse-amplitude modulation: the height follows the voice instead

onScreen: A normal moment for each pulse
Voice shifts it earlier or later
Signal varies the time each pulse occurs
scenes.narration: Next, pulse-position modulation, or PPM. Now every pulse is identical: same width, same height. Each one has a normal moment when it would occur, and the voice nudges it a little earlier or a little later, by an amount set by the voice at that instant. So in a pulse-position modulation system, the modulating signal varies the time at which each pulse occurs, while pulse width and amplitude stay constant. Think of a drummer keeping a steady beat but playing each hit slightly ahead of or behind it. The third method is the simplest: pulse-amplitude modulation, where the pulse heights follow the voice, and width and timing stay fixed.

Here are the 3 side by side, because the exam's wrong answers come from mixing them up. Pulse-width, or pulse-duration, modulation varies how long each pulse lasts. So when a pulse-width question offers pulse frequency, pulse amplitude or pulse intensity, pick duration instead. Pulse-position modulation varies when each pulse occurs: the answer is the time at which each pulse occurs, not the number of pulses per second or their duration. Pulse-amplitude modulation varies how tall each pulse is. Takeaway: width is how long, position is when, amplitude is how tall.

params.title: Peak power versus average power
labels: Short pulses separated by long off periods
Duty cycle: the fraction of the time it's on
Peak power: the power during a pulse
Average power = peak power × duty cycle

onScreen: Duty cycle: fraction of time on
Peak power: power during a pulse
scenes.narration: Pulses also change how we think about power, the rate at which a transmitter sends out energy, measured in watts. A pulse transmitter is on only during each short pulse, then off for a long gap before the next. The fraction of the time it's on is called the duty cycle. The power while a pulse is on is the peak power. Spread over time, though, the long gaps pull the power way down: the average power equals the peak power times the duty cycle. Radar is the classic example: brief, powerful pulses, with long gaps between them to listen for the echoes.

params.title: Worked example: average power
params.formula: Average power = peak power × duty cycle
steps: Duty cycle: on 1 part in 1000 of the time
Check: it's off almost all the time, so tiny fits
params.answer: Peak power is much greater than average power

onScreen: Average power = peak power × duty cycle
On 1 part in 1000 of the time
scenes.narration: Let's put numbers on it. Suppose a pulse transmitter's peak power is 1000 watts. It's on for just 1 part in 1000 of the time, so its duty cycle is 1 in 1000. To find the average power, multiply the peak power by the duty cycle: 1000 watts times 1 over 1000 is just 1 watt. Does that make sense? The transmitter is off almost all the time, so yes, the average should be tiny. That rules out the choices with the average only slightly below the peak, or the peak twice the average, and the SSB voice choice doesn't describe how a pulse system works. The right description: in a pulse modulation system, the peak transmitter power is normally much greater than the average power.

blocks.label: Sample
blocks.note: Measure the wave at regular instants

blocks.label: Code
blocks.note: Turn each measurement into a number

blocks.label: On-off pulses
blocks.note: Send each number as a pulse pattern

onScreen: Each sample turned into a number
scenes.narration: Back to carrying a voice. One more pulse method, pulse-code modulation, or PCM, goes a step further. It still samples the voice at regular instants, but instead of changing a pulse's height, width or timing, it measures each sample and turns it into a number. That number is sent as a code: a pattern of pulses that are simply on or off, the way computers store numbers. The receiver reads each pattern, turns it back into a measurement, and rebuilds the voice. Noise, the random hiss and crackle picked up along the way, can blur a pulse's height or width, but it rarely turns on into off. So PCM shrugs off a lot of noise.

blocks.label: One shared link
blocks.note: One frequency, kept apart by time

onScreen: Each sample in its own time slot, in turn
One shared link, kept apart by time
scenes.narration: PCM also makes it easy for many conversations to share one link. Each conversation is a channel: say channels 1, 2 and 3. Time-division multiplex lets them take turns. Multiplex means sending several channels over one link, and time division means each gets its own share of the time. A sample from channel 1 goes out in its own short time slot, then one from channel 2, then one from channel 3, and then round again, like dealing cards around a table. So all 3 share one link, on one frequency, kept apart only by time. The turns come so fast that each conversation still sounds continuous.

blocks.label: Transmit clock
blocks.note: Puts each sample in its time slot

scenes.narration: Taking turns only works if both ends agree on whose turn it is. A clock, a circuit that ticks out steady timing pulses, sets the time slots at the transmitter. At the far end, a clock at the receiver deals the samples back out to the right channels. So the important factor in pulse-code modulation using time-division multiplex is synchronization of the transmit and receive clock pulse rates, meaning the 2 clocks are kept in step. If they drift apart, samples land in the wrong time slots and the channels are scrambled. Frequency separation is the wrong choice: these channels share one frequency and are kept apart by time.

params.title: Key facts to remember
items: Deviation ratio = max deviation ÷ highest audio: 1.66 and 2.14
Modulation index varies; deviation ratio is fixed
FM: audio into the oscillator. DSB: modulate a class C amplifier's supply
Figure 3H17: audio in at block 2, block 4 mixer; test SSB with 2 tones
Pulses: width = duration, position = timing, peak ≫ average, clocks in sync

onScreen: FM and DSB: how they're made
Pulses: width, position, peak power, clocks
scenes.narration: To wrap up, here's what to remember. The deviation ratio is maximum deviation divided by the highest audio frequency, deviation on top: 5 over 3 is 1.66, and 7.5 over 3.5 is 2.14. The modulation index is the same kind of ratio at a given time, so it varies, while the deviation ratio is fixed. FM comes from feeding audio straight to the oscillator, and double sideband from modulating a class C amplifier's supply voltage. In Figure 3H17, audio goes in at block 2, and block 4, the mixer, marks an SSB transmitter, tested for linearity with 2 tones on an oscilloscope. In pulse modulation, width means duration, position means timing, peak power far exceeds average power, and time-division multiplex needs synchronized clocks.
